issues.title: Order and arguments of `@staticmethod` and `torch.compile()` decorators produces different results
issues.author: I-Absolutely-Am-Not-A-Robot
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Using the following base code :

```py3
class Foo(L.LightningModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, x):
        foo = Foo.foo(x)
        bar = Foo.bar(x)

        foobar = foo + bar
        return foobar

    def bar(x):
        return x
 
    def foo(x):
        return x
    
foo = Foo()
bar = foo(torch.Tensor([0]))

print(bar)
```

The following changes to function `bar` work :
```py3
    # OK
    @staticmethod
    @torch.compile()
    def bar(x):
        return x

    # OK
    @torch.compile()
    @staticmethod
    def bar(x):
        return x
```
```
Output: tensor([0.])
```
But this one raises an error :
```py3
    # Not OK
    @torch.compile(fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)
    @staticmethod
    def bar(x):
        return x
```

issues.title: [RFC] Inductor / AOTI tests: decouple “correct codegen path” from tight eager-fp16 equality
issues.author: iupaikov-amd
issues.body:
## 1. Summary

- Many Inductor and AOTI tests **prove two things at once**: (a) the **compiled path** matches the scenario we care about, and (b) **eager fp16** matches **compiled fp16** to a very tight tolerance. Those goals are often unrelated.
- When eager/compiled check fails on one vendor or SKU while the logic path is fine, we get **noise in CI and review**: skips, tolerance PRs, and repeated explanation - without strengthening the signal for the original regression.
- **fp16** is usually a **red herring**: the interesting question is often **routing, grid, or reference choice**, not “bit-identical GEMM across every math backend.”
- **Dedicated suites already cover fp16 matmul accuracy** (OpInfo, matmul tests). Re-encoding the same bar in **narrow integration tests** duplicates work and **varies by architecture** (e.g. different reduction tiling across GPUs).
- **Ask:** treat this as an incremental cleanup opportunity — tests that were reasonable when written can be upgraded to match the failure mode (structure, reference dtype, or codegen hints) while staying **vendor-neutral**.

---

## 2. Example: `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` (AOTI BMM, large dynamic batch)

- PR [#178617](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/178617) introduced logic: **dynamic** batch BMM with **`B > 65535`** must **launch legally** and **index batches correctly** (Triton batch split across `grid_y` / `grid_z`). This logic is checked by comparing if eager vs compiled outputs are bitwise identical. While this in theory covers the regression, it also is prone to 1 ULP fp16 jitter due to reordering on different archs. 
- [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) scaled inputs to reduce benign fp16 noise for CUDA, which is essentially a tolerance increase in disguise. This makes the test less flaky for **some** archs, but doesn't solve the root of the issue.
- Tight **`same()`** / eager-fp16 equality is **stricter than the bug** needs and **varies by hardware** (e.g. [#179958](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/179958), [#184531](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/184531)) — **false failures** even when the **grid fix** is sound.

---

## 3. Other examples (same pattern family)

| Link | Note |
|------|------|
| [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) | `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` — input scaling / tolerance / CUDA follow-up |
| [#184531](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/184531) | `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` — tolerance / ROCm follow-up |
| [#182028](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/182028) | ROCm MI200 — flex vs SDPA `assert_close` tolerances |
| [#186889](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/186889) | XPU — relaxed `assertEqual` vs eager (atomic ordering) |
| [#169694](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/169694) | Transformer tests — **golden** precision / reference choice |
| [#183691](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183691) | Test infra — tolerance overrides (helps **symptoms**; root cause is still design in individual tests) |

---

## 4. Conclusion & proposed next steps

- We would like to advocate for having some sort of test design guidelines to avoid such problems in the future and help to redesign some of the existing tests. Since this problem is universal for all vendors and multitude of archs we would like to bring this to your attention. As Inductor and hardware diversity grow, **narrowing the logic** per test is a good way to move forward.
- **Proposals (pick per test):**
  - **Match logic to risk:** grid / launch bugs → **shape, finiteness, boundary indices**, optional **codegen / log substring**; fp16 GEMM agreement → **leave to OpInfo / matmul** suites or use **FP32 reference + documented tol**.
  - **Tier or split checks:** small-shape **strict** + large-shape **reference-based**, so one failure mode doesn’t block the other.
  - **Document intent in-test** (one comment): what regression file / PR motivated the scenario—helps future edits stay aligned.
- **Proposed direction:** **FP32 matmul reference** (or similar), **boundary row checks** around **65535**, optional **Inductor log / codegen hints** for the batch reconstruction — **same regression intent**, **less coupling** to eager fp16 BLAS. I will link a draft PR to highlight what was described.

issues.title: [ONNX] Dynamo export freezes dynamic time dimension in manual bidirectional LSTM/GRU pattern
issues.author: SouperDuper
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=True)` exports a manual bidirectional LSTM or GRU pattern with a dynamic time axis, but the generated ONNX graph contains the example input time length in an internal `Expand` shape.

The exported model runs in ONNX Runtime for the example length, then fails for a different valid time length.

The same pattern works with `torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=False)`.

The control cases in the full reproducer show that these related cases work with `dynamo=True`:

- bare unidirectional `nn.LSTM`
- bare unidirectional `nn.GRU`
- masked unidirectional `nn.LSTM`
- masked unidirectional `nn.GRU`

The clean reproduction environment used the CUDA 13.0 PyTorch wheel, but the reproducer itself executes entirely on CPU and uses ONNX Runtime's `CPUExecutionProvider`.

### Reproduction

Full reproducer (script + requirements.txt): https://gist.github.com/SouperDuper/d00d4e94e4461f9fc3c08bf7815d32fe

The full reproducer above imports only PyTorch, ONNX, ONNX Script, ONNX Runtime, NumPy, and standard-library modules. It adds LSTM and GRU control cases, compares the legacy exporter, and inspects the generated graph for literal Expand dimensions.

The slightly smaller reproducer below shows narrower failing case plus the `dynamo=False` comparison.

Run: `python filename.py`

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import tempfile
import logging
from contextlib import redirect_stderr, redirect_stdout
from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import onnxruntime as ort
import torch


logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

def reverse_valid_prefix(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    key_padding_mask: torch.Tensor,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    lengths = (~key_padding_mask).to(dtype=torch.long).sum(dim=1)
    positions = torch.ones_like(key_padding_mask, dtype=torch.long).cumsum(dim=1) - 1
    reversed_positions = lengths.unsqueeze(1) - 1 - positions
    source_positions = torch.where(
        positions < lengths.unsqueeze(1),
        reversed_positions,
        positions,
    ).clamp_min(0)
    return x.gather(1, source_positions.unsqueeze(-1).expand_as(x))


class ManualBidirectionalLstm(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.forward_rnn = torch.nn.LSTM(
            input_size=16,
            hidden_size=8,
            num_layers=1,
            batch_first=True,
            bidirectional=False,
            dropout=0.0,
        )
        self.backward_rnn = torch.nn.LSTM(
            input_size=16,
            hidden_size=8,
            num_layers=1,
            batch_first=True,
            bidirectional=False,
            dropout=0.0,
        )
        self.output = torch.nn.Linear(16, 16)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, key_padding_mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        forward, _ = self.forward_rnn(x)
        backward_input = reverse_valid_prefix(x, key_padding_mask)
        backward_reversed, _ = self.backward_rnn(backward_input)
        backward = reverse_valid_prefix(backward_reversed, key_padding_mask)
        return self.output(torch.cat((forward, backward), dim=-1))


def export_model(path: Path, *, dynamo: bool) -> None:
    model = ManualBidirectionalLstm().eval()
    x = torch.randn((1, 6, 16), dtype=torch.float32)
    key_padding_mask = torch.zeros((1, 6), dtype=torch.bool)

    kwargs = {
        "dynamo": dynamo,
        "external_data": False,
        "input_names": ["x", "key_padding_mask"],
        "output_names": ["y"],
        "opset_version": 18,
    }
    if dynamo:
        kwargs["dynamic_shapes"] = {
            "x": {0: torch.export.Dim.AUTO, 1: torch.export.Dim.AUTO},
            "key_padding_mask": {0: torch.export.Dim.AUTO, 1: torch.export.Dim.AUTO},
        }
    else:
        kwargs["dynamic_axes"] = {
            "x": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
            "key_padding_mask": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
            "y": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
        }

    with redirect_stdout(StringIO()), redirect_stderr(StringIO()):
        torch.onnx.export(model, (x, key_padding_mask), path, **kwargs)


def run_onnx(path: Path, *, n_frames: int) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    session_options = ort.SessionOptions()
    session_options.log_severity_level = 4
    session = ort.InferenceSession(
        path.as_posix(),
        sess_options=session_options,
        providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"],
    )
    feeds = {
        "x": np.random.randn(1, n_frames, 16).astype(np.float32),
        "key_padding_mask": np.zeros((1, n_frames), dtype=np.bool_),
    }
    try:
        session.run(None, feeds)
    except Exception as exc:
        return False, str(exc).splitlines()[0]
    return True, ""


def main() -> None:
    torch.manual_seed(1234)
    output_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="onnx-dynamo-bidir-rnn-"))

    dynamo_path = output_dir / "manual_bidirectional_lstm.dynamo.onnx"
    export_model(dynamo_path, dynamo=True)
    dynamo_t6_ok, dynamo_t6_error = run_onnx(dynamo_path, n_frames=6)
    dynamo_t9_ok, dynamo_t9_error = run_onnx(dynamo_path, n_frames=9)

    legacy_path = output_dir / "manual_bidirectional_lstm.legacy.onnx"
    export_model(legacy_path, dynamo=False)
    legacy_t9_ok, legacy_t9_error = run_onnx(legacy_path, n_frames=9)

    print(f"dynamo_t6={'ok' if dynamo_t6_ok else 'fail'} error={dynamo_t6_error!r}")
    print(f"dynamo_t9={'ok' if dynamo_t9_ok else 'fail'} error={dynamo_t9_error!r}")
    print(f"legacy_t9={'ok' if legacy_t9_ok else 'fail'} error={legacy_t9_error!r}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Actual output

Narrower reproducer:

```text
dynamo_t6=ok error=''
dynamo_t9=fail error="[ONNXRuntimeError] : 2 : INVALID_ARGUMENT : Non-zero status code returned while running Expand node. Name:'node_expand_1' Status Message: invalid expand shape"
legacy_t9=ok error=''
```

Full reproducer:

```text
output_dir=<tempdir>
python=3.11.14
torch=2.12.1+cu130
onnx=1.22.0
onnxscript=0.7.1
onnxruntime=1.28.0
numpy=1.26.4
lstm_bare: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=ok error=''
lstm_masked_unidirectional: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=ok error=''
lstm_manual_bidirectional: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=fail error="[ONNXRuntimeError] : 2 : INVALID_ARGUMENT : Non-zero status code returned while running Expand node. Name:'node_expand_1' Status Message: invalid expand shape"
lstm_manual_bidirectional: legacy_export=ok legacy_ort_t9=ok error='' dynamo_expand_shape_literals=[[1, 8], [16], [6, 8]]
gru_bare: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=ok error=''
gru_masked_unidirectional: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=ok error=''
gru_manual_bidirectional: dynamo_export=ok dynamo_ort_t6=ok dynamo_ort_t9=fail error="[ONNXRuntimeError] : 2 : INVALID_ARGUMENT : Non-zero status code returned while running Expand node. Name:'node_expand_1' Status Message: invalid expand shape"
gru_manual_bidirectional: legacy_export=ok legacy_ort_t9=ok error='' dynamo_expand_shape_literals=[[1, 8], [16], [6, 8]]
```

The model is exported with an example input of shape `[1, 6, 16]`.

The repro only validates dynamic time behavior. It does not claim dynamic batch behavior, because the example batch size and test batch size are both `1`.

The public input time axis accepts a different length in the working cases. In the failing manual bidirectional cases from the full reproducer, the ONNX graph still contains the literal `6` in an internal `Expand` shape:

```text
dynamo_expand_shape_literals=[[1, 8], [16], [6, 8]]
```

This makes the exported model invalid for a different time length, such as `[1, 9, 16]`.

### Expected behavior

If `dynamo=True` export succeeds with a dynamic time axis, the exported ONNX model should run with a different valid sequence length.

The manual bidirectional LSTM and GRU cases should behave like the passing cases:

- export from `[1, 6, 16]`
- run in ONNX Runtime with `[1, 6, 16]`
- run in ONNX Runtime with `[1, 9, 16]`

### Why this looks like an exporter bug

The failing model is ordinary PyTorch code:

- two unidirectional `nn.LSTM` or `nn.GRU` modules
- `torch.gather` with a mask-derived reverse index
- `torch.cat`
- `torch.nn.Linear`

The same bidirectional model works with `torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=False)`.

The bare RNN and masked unidirectional cases in the full reproducer also work with `dynamo=True`.

The failure is not ONNX Runtime rejecting the public input shape. ONNX Runtime accepts the dynamic public input, then fails inside the graph because a shape derived from the export example length is frozen into an internal `Expand`.

> **AI-assistance disclosure:** I do not have experience writing proper bug reports, so I used ChatGPT to help package and organize this report. I personally wrote the original failure case, ran the reproducer, reviewed the code and exported graphs, and verified the technical claims and reported output. AI was a sanity check, but it tends to make the resulting report too wordy.

issues.title: [Inductor] Question: schedule-aware multi-stream orchestration in generated wrapper code
issues.author: joozhan
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Hi PyTorch team,

I would like to ask whether there has been any discussion or planned work around automatic or semi-automatic multi-stream orchestration in TorchInductor-generated code.

From my current understanding, the recent user-stream related work in torch.compile mainly focuses on preserving explicit stream/event semantics written by users, for example:

s = torch.cuda.Stream()
with torch.cuda.stream(s):
    y = some_op(x)

torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)

That is, the compiler should not drop or incorrectly reorder user-defined stream contexts, events, or wait_stream dependencies.

What I am interested in is a slightly different direction:

After Inductor lowering/fusion/scheduling, can Inductor assign some scheduled nodes or generated kernels to different CUDA streams and generate the required stream/event synchronization in the output wrapper code?

For example, given a graph with independent branches:

a = branch_a(x)
b = branch_b(y)
out = combine(a, b)

Inductor could theoretically generate code similar to:
```
 # stream 0
branch_a_kernel(...)

# stream 1
branch_b_kernel(...)

# join
main_stream.wait_stream(stream0)
main_stream.wait_stream(stream1)

combine_kernel(...)
```
I understand that doing this correctly is non-trivial. A robust implementation would likely need to be schedule-aware rather than a simple post-processing pass over generated Python code. It would need access to information such as:

buffer read/write dependencies
aliasing and mutation information
fusion boundaries
external kernel / ATen op boundaries
buffer lifetime and memory reuse
CUDA Graph compatibility
stream pool / stream count control
cost model decisions about when parallelism is actually beneficial

A possible MVP could be much narrower than a general DAG scheduler, for example:

only handle two or more independent branches
only allow read-only shared inputs
disallow mutation / aliasing / in-place writes
avoid CUDA Graph / reduce-overhead mode initially
emit explicit events or wait_stream calls in the generated wrapper
use a small fixed number of auxiliary streams
gate the behavior behind an experimental config flag

Pseudo-shape of the implementation:

FX graph
  -> Inductor lowering / fusion / scheduling
  -> dependency + liveness analysis
  -> assign stream_id to selected scheduled nodes
  -> wrapper codegen emits stream/event orchestration

This would be different from the existing user-stream support: instead of only preserving user-authored stream semantics, Inductor would create stream-level parallelism for selected patterns where the dependencies are known to be safe.

My questions are:

Has TorchInductor considered schedule-aware multi-stream code generation before?
Are there existing blockers in Inductor’s scheduler, memory planner, CUDA Graph integration, or wrapper codegen that would make this direction impractical?
Would the PyTorch team be open to an experimental, pattern-based implementation behind a config flag?
Is there a preferred layer where such stream assignment should live: FX graph, Inductor scheduler, wrapper codegen, or somewhere else?
Are there known benchmarks or model patterns where the team believes this could be useful, such as independent compute branches, copy/compute overlap, or communication/compute overlap?

I would be happy to learn whether this direction aligns with the compiler roadmap, and whether there are recommended starting points in the codebase for prototyping this.

### Alternatives

_No response_

comments.author: CodersAcademy006
comments.body: Most of the dependency information such a pass needs already lives in the Inductor scheduler rather than the FX graph: `SchedulerNode` tracks read/write/star deps, mutation and aliasing, and the memory planner already computes buffer liveness and reuse, so the scheduler (`torch/_inductor/scheduler.py`) is the natural layer to assign a stream id, while wrapper codegen (`torch/_inductor/codegen/wrapper.py`) is where the `record_event`/`wait_stream` calls would be emitted. The FX graph is too early (no fusion or buffer info) and a post-pass over generated Python is too late, as you note. The two real blockers are CUDA Graphs and the cost model. `cudagraph_trees` assumes a single capture stream, so multi-stream would have to be gated off under reduce-overhead/cudagraph mode initially, which matches your MVP scope. The cost model is the harder half: a single stream already saturates the SMs for most compute-bound kernels, so extra streams only pay off when the independent branches are small and launch/latency bound, or when it is copy/compute or comm/compute overlap, where `reorder_for_compute_comm_overlap` is the closest existing prior art. A config-gated experimental pass restricted to read-only shared inputs, no mutation or aliasing, and non-cudagraph mode looks tractable and fits how the scheduler already reasons about deps.
